Keywords: while he lives

outputs.L1:

while he lives, here's a list of images: light diffused through a grimy pane, a pigeon dead atop the spiked window, a clear plastic bag suspended above him, brimming with water—as if water alone could drown everything living inside you, and it can. i sit in a corner of the cancer ward, thumbing an app that reveals other faggots scattered through this hospital, chatting with one i might encounter in radiology, but don't. instead, i make the sick man laugh while he's still conscious, praising his gown, his new cheekbones carved brutal by the chemo. if only it were as simple as a magnet drawing the poisoned metals from his blood. if only i could compose a truer list—more magic, less language, less periphrasis, more restoration. if only i met that stranger in the basement, and our pleasure rose through the hospital like a poultice for the sorrow-skinned, those who sit half-conscious, half-machine. while the sick man lives, all i can do is chronicle the vast pastoral of his illness. when he is gone, i'll be counting on all that goodness flooding back—his beard, a collapsed country i'll take refuge in; his laugh, a memory so fluid i'll hear it still, whenever someone opens a window to startle the birds.
outputs.L2:
Here's my rewrite, preserving the imagery and narrative while restructuring the language:

---

While he's still with us, here's an inventory of what I see: light filtering through a smudged pane, a pigeon's corpse impaled on the window's metal spikes, and above it, a transparent bag swollen with water—as if liquid alone could drown every living cell inside you, and maybe it could. I position myself in a corner of the oncology unit, thumbing through an app that reveals which other queer men occupy this building. There's someone I could message, someone I might cross paths with down in radiology, but I hold back. Instead, I focus on making him smile while he's still lucid, praising his hospital gown, remarking on the sharp new angles of his face that chemotherapy has carved. I wish removing the poison were as effortless as a magnet drawing out corrupted metal. I wish I could compose something better than this list—more enchantment, less explanation, something roundabout yet healing. I wish I'd actually met that stranger downstairs, let our shared pleasure spread like warmth through these corridors, a soothing balm for all of us with grief-worn skin, suspended between awareness and the machines keeping us tethered. As long as he's alive, all I can offer is this sprawling account of his sickness. Once he's no longer here, I'll depend on the good memories rushing back—his beard like a nation that's fallen, a place I'll seek shelter in; his laughter, a sound so fluid I'll imagine hearing it whenever a window cracks open and startles the birds outside.
outputs.L3:
# Waiting Room

The fluorescent lights hum overhead in the cancer ward, casting everything in that particular hospital pallor that makes even healthy skin look sallow. I sit in a plastic chair, my mind cataloging fragments of the world outside the window with the detached precision of someone trying not to think too hard about where they are. A dead pigeon lies motionless on the windowsill of the building across the way, its stillness somehow more pronounced against the gray concrete. Below, in the parking lot, a plastic bag has caught on a chain-link fence, filled with rainwater, bulging and precarious, threatening to burst or fall at any moment. These images arrange themselves into a private language of mortality—small, grim tableaux that mirror the larger drama unfolding in the rooms around me.

To distract myself, I open a dating app on my phone, and there they are: other queer men, their profiles pinging within these same walls. It's a strange intimacy, knowing that somewhere in radiology, someone else is scrolling through the same grid of faces, killing the same anxious hours. I imagine, briefly, what it might be like to meet him—a stolen conversation in a stairwell, a shared cigarette outside the emergency entrance, some flicker of connection amid all this sterility and fear. But I close the app without messaging him. The moment doesn't belong to me right now.

Instead, I turn back to the man beside me—the one whose treatment has brought us both to this place—and I try to make him laugh. I tell him his eyes look sharper now, more striking against the smoothness of his bald head, that the chemotherapy has stripped away everything unnecessary and left something almost elemental. He laughs, weakly but genuinely, and for a moment the sterile air feels lighter. This is what I can offer: not distraction from illness, but tenderness within it.

Still, some part of me aches for something impossible—a simpler cure, something almost fairy-tale in its ease, a touch or a word that could undo the damage cell by cell. In the absence of that magic, I let myself imagine, just for a heartbeat, an alternate version of this day: anonymous pleasure with a stranger, urgent and thoughtless, a small rebellion against the heaviness pressing down on every hallway and waiting room. It would be so easy to disappear into that fantasy, to borrow someone else's body as an escape from the fragility of the one I love.

But I don't. I understand, with a clarity that feels almost brutal, the limits of what I'm able to give while he is still here—still laughing, still speaking, still turning his changed face toward mine. So I stay. I memorize the sound of his laughter, the ghost of his beard now growing back in patches, the specific way he exists in this moment, in this room, in this light. These are the things I will carry forward, the fragments I will assemble into memory once he is gone—not as replacement for his presence, but as the only shelter I'll have against its absence.
outputs.L4:
# Ward 6B, or: Grindr for the Terminal

The app says *0.2 miles away*—
which is to say: through two walls,
past the nurses' station, next to the ice machine
that hums like it's dying too.

*Into: fentanyl drips, bad puns, watching Jeopardy reruns.*
*Not into: pity, small talk about my numbers.*

I make a list because lists are all I can hold:
his laugh, cracked at the edges like old paint.
His beard, unshaved for eleven days,
gone gray in places it wasn't gray in June.
The way he calls the chemo bag *Janet*
because she never leaves, because she's always dripping
something into him that isn't love
but has to do for now.

Dark humor is a rope you throw yourself
when the water's already in your lungs.
*What do you call a man with no hair and four IVs?*
*Still here. Still here. Still—*

I swipe through faces in the waiting room app—
a joke I made, a world I built
where someone two floors down in Oncology
wants to know my astrological sign
instead of my next of kin.
Where flirting is a kind of prayer
that doesn't require God,
just the audacity to want
something other than survival.

I write him poems he's too tired to read.
I say *I love you* in fourteen different tenses—
past, present, the conditional
of a future we won't get.
None of it shrinks the tumor.
None of it thins the blood enough
for one more good vein.

Language was never the cure.
I know this now, the way you know
a door is locked before you try the handle.
All I can do is stand here
in the fluorescent dark,
memorizing:

his laugh (the real one, before the pain took the octave)
his beard (soft, gone silver, smelling like the soap
his mother used to buy him)
the way he said *okay, okay* like a lullaby
each time they came to draw more blood.

I am building a museum
out of a man while he's still breathing.
I am learning the difference
between witness and rescue.

One is a hand. The other is a myth.

When he's gone—and some nights I let myself
say *when*, just to practice the shape of it in my mouth—
I will still have this:
the laugh, cracked and generous.
The beard, rough against my palm.
Small relics. Enough to build a chapel
out of what's left,
enough to kneel in.
outputs.L5:
# While He Lives

There is a peculiar weight carried in those three words: while he lives. They mark a boundary, a temporary permission, an understanding that some arrangement—some peace, some silence, some tolerance—exists only within the span of a single life, and will end when that life does.

Families speak this way about inheritances and promises. "The house stays as it is, while he lives." Kingdoms and courts have used the phrase for centuries, granting titles or lands with the unspoken addendum that everything reverts, changes, or dissolves upon a death. It is a phrase that acknowledges mortality without naming it directly—a way of gesturing toward the end without having to speak the word itself.

There is something almost merciful in this indirection. To say "while he lives" is to hold two truths together: that the present arrangement matters, and that it is not permanent. It lets people plan around uncertainty. It offers a kind of grace to those who wait—an heir, a rival, a quiet dissenter—by giving their waiting a shape, a horizon, even if that horizon cannot be dated.

But the phrase also carries a darker undertone. It can imply resentment, patience worn thin, a peace enforced rather than chosen. "While he lives, we say nothing." "While he lives, the matter cannot be settled." These are the words of people counting days without admitting they are counting, of loyalties that are really just deferrals.

And yet there is tenderness in the phrase too, when spoken by those who love. A promise to visit, to care for, to remain—while he lives—becomes not a countdown but a vow: for as long as this time lasts, I am here. Not forever, because forever is not available to any of us. But wholly, for the time that is given.

Perhaps that is the quiet lesson tucked inside these three words. They do not pretend at permanence. They ask only for presence—for as long as presence is possible. In accepting the limit, they somehow deepen the meaning of what falls within it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, image-driven prose poem about visiting a boyfriend with cancer in the hospital, mixing dark humor with grief and queer desire.
counterfactuals.output:
# Visiting Hours

The IV pole is the ugliest houseplant I've ever tended. You call it Steve. Steve drips into you like a broken faucet nobody fixed, and I bring grapes nobody eats because what are we, a Victorian painting? *Still Life With Boyfriend, Dying, Slightly.*

Your hospital gown gapes at the back and I want you anyway, want you with the tubes and the beeping and the particular blue of your lips after they draw blood, want you in this bed that smells like antiseptic and the ghost of someone else's cafeteria Jell-O. Desire doesn't check the charts. Desire doesn't care that your hair is coming out in the sink like a bad breakup, fistfuls of you going down the drain while I watch and think *I would eat you whole if it meant keeping something.*

You make jokes about becoming a skeleton early, beating the rush. "Efficient," you say. "Very German of me." Your laugh is a wet engine trying to turn over. I laugh too because the alternative is a sound I don't have a name for yet, something between a scream and a prayer, and prayer isn't really our language, is it? We speak in dick jokes and playlist links and the specific dialect of two boys who found each other and thought *oh, there you are* — not *finally* but *of course.*

The nurse with kind eyes calls us "you two" like it's obvious, like it doesn't need footnotes, and something in my chest unclenches every time she does it. Small mercies. Steve drips. You sleep sometimes mid-sentence, a magic trick, here then not-here, and I sit in the plastic chair that's shaped like nothing human and watch your chest for the rise, the proof, the small miracle of continuance.

I kiss your temple where they shaved a strip for the surgery, the skin new and shocked-looking, a bald patch like a monk's tonsure. Sacred, maybe. Or just skin. I don't know anymore where the line is between reverence and just wanting you alive, wanting you *here*, wanting your hand which is still your hand, still knows how to hold mine like we're not in a room that smells like dying, like we're just two idiots on a Tuesday, in love, in a chair shaped like nothing, waiting for grapes to matter.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem narrated by someone sitting in a cancer ward with a sick partner, incorporating hookup app culture, body imagery, and anticipatory mourning.
counterfactuals.output:
**Visiting Hours**

The vitals monitor keeps a rhythm
I could dance to, if dancing
were still a thing bodies did
in this room instead of trembling.

Your arm is a garden of bruises,
blue and yellow blooming
where they've dug for a vein
that keeps hiding, shy,
the way you used to hide your face
when I first said I loved it —
the soft slope of your belly,
the scar over your eyebrow
from a childhood I never got to see.

I open the app because my hands
need something to do
that isn't holding yours too hard,
isn't counting your breaths
like sheep I'm begging not to jump
the fence into forever.

Grid of torsos. Grid of jaws.
*Distance: 0.3 miles.* Someone near
is hosting, is hard, is looking
right now — an economy of wanting
that never asks how you're feeling,
never charts your temperature,
never once says *I might lose you.*

I used to be a body like that —
a thumbnail, a maybe, a six-pack
of promises I didn't keep.
Now I am a chair beside a bed.
Now I am a hand that forgets
what it's like to reach for skin
that isn't tethered to a pole.

The nurse says *good veins, bad luck.*
I think: that's us. That's the whole
love story, condensed to a chart.

I close the app. I open it again.
Somewhere a stranger is beautiful
and uncomplicated and I hate him
for the sin of being only that —
a body without an ending scheduled,
a mouth I could kiss
without tasting the metal
of what's coming.

Already I am practicing your absence
the way you practice scales
before a recital — clumsy,
too early, humiliating.
I fold your sweater in the closet
at home, already a relic.
I say your name out loud
just to hear it still attached
to breath, to a room,
to a body that hasn't yet
become a story I tell.

Your hand finds mine
without opening your eyes.
The monitor keeps its rhythm.
Somewhere my phone lights up
with a stranger's hunger
and I let it go dark
in my pocket, un-answered,
the way I wish I could let go
of the arithmetic in my chest
that's already counting
the days you have left
like a man counting coins
he knows won't be enough,
spending them anyway —
here, now, on your knuckles,
on the small miracle
of your thumb moving
against mine —

still warm,
still yours,
still, for now,
here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem with no punctuation that explores caregiving, illness, and queer intimacy, using surreal metaphors like pigeons, magnets, and windows.
counterfactuals.output:
**what the window knows**

your fever speaks a language made of pigeons
gray syllables landing on the sill each morning
asking to be let in asking to be fed
i open my palm like a window opens
like a mouth that forgot how to close

i learned to love you the way magnets learn distance
how something invisible keeps two bodies
almost touching almost touching
never quite arriving at the skin
this is what they don't tell you about devotion
it is mostly the space between

your hands today are cold coins
i warm them in my mouth like a secret
the doctor says words i turn into weather
partly cloudy with a chance of your name
disappearing from your own tongue

the pigeons keep gathering on the sill
i think they are rehearsing goodbye
i think they are just hungry
i think i am the only different from birds

we built a house out of appointments and pills
out of your hand finding my hand in the dark
like a compass finding a direction
that was never north just toward

some nights i am the magnet and you are the metal
some nights it reverses and i am pulled toward your breathing
just to make sure it is still a sound
still a small machine of continuing

the window holds our reflection badly
doubles us into ghosts who might be kissing
might be arguing might be the same gesture
love and fear wearing each other's coats

i feed the pigeons your leftover bread
i tell them you are still here
i tell them this every morning
like a ritual like a magnet
like the window that keeps letting light in
whether or not we are ready for it

some days your body forgets what it promised
some days i forget i am allowed to be tired
we are both learning the physics of holding on
how everything attracted eventually
becomes its own kind of gravity

the pigeons do not judge us
for loving strange for loving sick
for loving in the space between two magnets
where nothing touches
but nothing lets go either

this is the only prayer i know now
window open bread scattered
your hand a compass in mine
still pointing somewhere
still pointing toward
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness piece about loving someone through chemotherapy, blending tenderness, gallows humor, and the fear of loss.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Remembers

Your hair comes off in fistfuls now like October
leaving the trees and I say nothing about the trees
I say nothing about anything except *here, let me*
and hold the plastic bag like it's a small casket
for something that never had a chance to die properly—

this isn't a metaphor you tell me, laughing
that thin laugh that costs you now, everything costs you now,
even joy has a copay, even breathing
has a deductible we didn't know we signed up for
when the doctor said *aggressive* like it was a compliment,
like your cells were finally showing some ambition.

I count your pills like a rosary I don't believe in.
Steroid, anti-nausea, the one that makes you see
halos around every lamp, makes you swear
you saw your dead grandmother in the bathroom mirror
asking if you'd eaten. *Typical*, you said. *Even dead
she's worried about my weight.*

We make jokes because the alternative
is this apartment filling up with silence
like water finding every crack—

I lie awake and do the math I promised I wouldn't do:
subtract the good days from the bad days,
divide by the number of times you've said *I'm tired*
in a voice that means something larger than sleep,
multiply my fear by every 3 a.m.
I've stood in the doorway just to hear you breathing,
just to make sure the dark hadn't taken you
while I wasn't looking, while I was only human,
only capable of loving you in this small, insufficient way—

your body a battlefield and me just
someone bringing water to soldiers,
someone who can't stop the war
but can hold the cup steady,
can say *drink, just drink, that's it, good*

and mean it like a prayer,
mean it like the only prayer I know—

You laugh at the wig, say it makes you look
like a Bond villain's secretary, sexy and unhinged,
and I laugh too because we are both terrified
and this is what terror looks like sometimes—
absurd, tender, wearing a joke
like a coat two sizes too big
just to stay warm another hour,
just to stay
another hour,
just to stay.

I am learning the vocabulary of almost-loss:
*remission* like a held breath,
*prognosis* like weather I can't control,
*five-year survival rate* a phrase
I turn over and over like a stone
looking for the smooth side, the lucky side,
the side that doesn't cut.

But mostly I am learning this:
how to love you in the specific,
not the abstract—not *I love you forever*
but *I love you now, in this ugly light,
with this bucket beside the bed,
with your hand finding mine
even when you can't find the words,
even when the words have gone
the way of your hair, your appetite,
your certainty about tomorrow—

I love you in the particular grammar of survival,
present tense, no promises,
just this: *here. I'm here. Drink the water.
I'm not going anywhere.
Watch me not go anywhere.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in a confessional, avant-garde style about sitting beside a dying gay man, weaving together hospital detail, cruising apps, and elegiac longing.
counterfactuals.output:
**Last Seen**

*I.*
The monitor keeps a rhythm truer than any hymn—
green line stuttering across black
like a text he'll never finish typing.

I hold the plastic railing instead of his hand
because his hand has tubes running out of it
like roads leaving a city no one visits anymore.

*II.*
On my phone, still, some reflex older than grief:
a grid of faces. *Online now. 4,200 ft.*
Someone wants to know if I'm here for right now.

I am here for right now.
I am here for the antiseptic
braided with the ghost of poppers
that never fully leaves a man who lived like this.

*III.*
His profile said *discreet, host only, no drama*
and now the drama is a machine
counting his heartbeats down like a countdown clock
before the good part—except there is no good part,
just the long taper,
the way a hookup sometimes ends
not with a door closing
but with someone
just not answering anymore.

*IV.*
The nurse changes his catheter
with the tenderness of a man
who has learned tenderness is just another word for job.
I think of every man who touched him—
gently, roughly, briefly—in rooms like this
but with better lighting, better music,
an app glowing on the nightstand
like a votive candle
to some small god of *right now, right now, right now.*

*V.*
Someone taps his old profile today.
Ghost of a man not yet a ghost
still getting messages from strangers
who don't know the body they're asking for
is asking for nothing now
but morphine, and quiet, and me.

*VI.*
Elegy is just cruising for the dead—
scrolling through what's left,
checking the distance between us,
once measured in feet,
now measured in breaths,
in how long between them,
how the gaps widen
like the silence after someone
stops typing back.

*VII.*
I delete the apps from his phone
before his mother arrives.
Some mercy he'd want, even now:
to be remembered as wanted,
not only as dying.

*Online now. Online now.*
Until, some gray hour—
offline.
No status. No grid. No ping.
Just the shape of a man
who used to answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
